pharm: Competitively inhibits intestinal alpha-glucosidases (and pancreatic alpha-amylase), delaying carbohydrate digestion and blunting postprandial glucose rise.
quick: Start 25 mg three times daily; titrate up to max 100 mg three times daily
Take with the first bite of each main meal
Insulin preferred; use only if clearly needed
Avoid; small amounts may appear in milk
summary: Acarbose is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor used as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes. By delaying intestinal carbohydrate digestion, it lowers postprandial blood glucose with minimal systemic absorption. It commonly causes flatulence, diarrhea, and abdominal discomfort, which improve with slow titration. Used alone it does not cause hypoglycemia, but when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, hypoglycemia must be treated with oral glucose (not sucrose).
indications: Adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus

dosage.d: 25 mg three times daily with the first bite of each main meal
dosage.n: May start 25 mg once daily and titrate to limit GI effects

dosage.d: Increase at 4-8 week intervals to 50-100 mg three times daily based on response and tolerance

admin: Take with the first bite (first mouthful) of each main meal
Start at a low dose and escalate gradually to minimize gastrointestinal side effects
Use 1-hour postprandial plasma glucose to guide dose titration
Adhere to the prescribed diabetic diet to limit intestinal side effects
For hypoglycemia (when combined with insulin/sulfonylurea), use glucose (dextrose) - not table sugar (sucrose)
moa: Acarbose competitively and reversibly inhibits membrane-bound intestinal alpha-glucosidase enzymes (e.g., glucoamylase, sucrase, maltase) and, to a lesser extent, pancreatic alpha-amylase. This delays the hydrolysis of complex carbohydrates and disaccharides into absorbable monosaccharides, slowing glucose absorption and reducing the postprandial rise in blood glucose. Because its action is local in the gut and it is minimally absorbed, it does not stimulate insulin secretion or cause hypoglycemia by itself.

absolute: Partial intestinal obstruction or predisposition to obstruction
Chronic intestinal diseases with marked disorders of digestion or absorption
Conditions that may worsen with increased intestinal gas formation
relative: Renal impairment (serum creatinine >2 mg/dL - not recommended)

preg: There are no adequate human data; insulin is generally preferred for diabetes in pregnancy. Use acarbose during pregnancy only if clearly needed and the benefit justifies the risk.
lact: A small amount of radioactivity has appeared in the milk of lactating animals; it is not known whether acarbose is excreted in human milk. Because of potential effects, avoid use or do not breastfeed during therapy.
renal: Plasma concentrations of acarbose increase markedly in renal impairment; it is not recommended in patients with serum creatinine greater than 2 mg/dL.
hepatic: Contraindicated in cirrhosis. Dose-related elevations of serum transaminases can occur (more with doses >50 mg three times daily); monitor liver enzymes, especially during the first year, and discontinue if elevations persist.

major: Insulin or sulfonylureas - increased hypoglycemia risk (treat hypoglycemia with glucose, not sucrose)
moderate: Intestinal adsorbents (e.g., charcoal) and digestive enzyme preparations (amylase, pancreatin) - reduce acarbose effect; avoid concurrent use
Digoxin - acarbose may alter digoxin levels; monitor and adjust
Drugs causing hyperglycemia (corticosteroids, thiazides, estrogens, phenytoin, sympathomimetics) - may worsen control
minor: Metformin (acarbose may modestly reduce metformin bioavailability)
interactions.food: Must be taken with the first bite of each main meal; effect depends on dietary carbohydrate.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; it can disturb glycemic control.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause dose-related elevations of serum transaminases.

monitoring: Serum transaminases at baseline and periodically (especially first year)
counsel: Take each dose with the first bite of your main meals
Gas, bloating, and diarrhea are common at first and usually lessen over time
If you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea and have low blood sugar, use glucose tablets or gel - ordinary table sugar will not work quickly with this medicine
Keep to your prescribed diet to reduce stomach side effects
Attend regular blood tests, including liver function
pk: Acts within the gut at each meal
Minimal systemic absorption (<2% of active drug absorbed)
Effect spans each meal; dosed three times daily
Store at or below 25 C; protect from moisture
pearls: Targets postprandial hyperglycemia specifically and does not cause hypoglycemia when used alone
Treat hypoglycemia (in combination therapy) with glucose/dextrose, NOT sucrose - acarbose blocks sucrose breakdown
GI side effects (flatulence, diarrhea) are the main reason for discontinuation - titrate slowly
Monitor liver enzymes, especially in the first year and at higher doses
Avoid if serum creatinine >2 mg/dL and contraindicated in cirrhosis/IBD
missed: If you miss a dose at the start of a meal, you can take it during the meal; if the meal is finished, skip the dose and take the next one with your next meal. Do not double up.
overdose: An overdose taken with carbohydrate-containing food may cause transient increased flatulence, diarrhea, and abdominal discomfort; it does not cause hypoglycemia. Manage by avoiding carbohydrate-containing food/drink for 4-6 hours and providing supportive care.
